newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba reinforces coast patrols to monitor exiles.
newsitem.headline: Cuba reinforces coast patrols to monitor exiles.

text.p: Cuba reinforced patrols of its waters on Monday as Miami-based exiles flew near the island to mark the first anniversary of the downing by Cuban MiG fighters of two small planes flown by exiles.

In Miami the U.S. Coast Guard said a fleet of Cuban exile planes made its way safely back to Miami after dropping wreaths in the Florida Strait. The planes apparently flew to a point about 22 miles (35 km) off Cuba, in international waters, where the United States says the planes were downed on Feb. 24 1996.
The commemoration at sea passed without incident.
But in Havana leading Cuban political dissident, Vladimiro Roca, said Cuban police had detained 11 dissidents since Saturday. Eight of them were picked up on Monday, he said.
Roca told foreign correspondents in Havana the dissidents came from different groups and were detained in Havana, Santiago de Cuba and the eastern city of Guantanamo.
There was no independent confirmation of the reported detentions. Cuban authorities rarely confirm or deny the arrest of anti-government dissidents.
Roca said five of the 11 who were detained in Guantanamo had been planning to throw flowers into the sea to commemorate the downing of the U.S.-registered exile planes.

Cuba says the Cessna planes, operated by an exile group called Brothers to the Rescue, were shot down within Cuba's 12-mile (19 km) territorial limit. The four exile crew members were killed in the incident.

Several dozen local and foreign reporters, invited by Cuban authorities, traveled out to sea on a naval submarine chaser for what officials called an observation mission. It was not clear whether any other vessels took part in patrols.

The submarine chaser sailed to around 10 miles (16 km) north of Havana. From there, a U.S. Coast Guard vessel could be seen in the distant horizon. The U.S. vessel was at a point about 22 miles (35 km) north of Havana, marking the spot where the exile planes flew to drop their wreaths.
The Cuban Foreign Ministry, warning exile groups it would not tolerate territorial violations, had said last week Cuba would use any means necesary to prevent such violations.
The plane downings last year sparked international outrage led by Washington, which toughened its longstanding economic embargo on Cuba.
President Fidel Castro's government said it acted in legitimate self-defense. It said the planes were violating Cuban airspace when they were shot down and had ignored warnings to leave.
Washington said the incident was an act of brutality. It said the planes were over international waters and wherever they were, should not have been brought down with force.

The names of the four exiles killed in the incident were read out and remembered during a mass on Monday morning at one Havana church. The names, part of a customary list of people to be mourned, were apparently included by relatives.

Cuban authorities reiterated on Monday that the plane downings could have been prevented by the United States. An article in the weekly newspaper Trabajadores said Washington should have acted to prevent territorial violations by Cuban exile groups.

The newspaper noted that Cuba had clearly warned in January 1996 that it might use force to prevent territorial violations. It added U.S. authorities had been fully aware of the situation and of the exile group's plans, but had not acted.
